passage:
I've been at the company six years, and I sit across from Akash, who joined in January. Last week he was asked to set up the new visitor ID cards for our office.
On Monday he showed me his plan on a single sheet: order blank cards Monday, print Tuesday, go live Wednesday. He looked pleased. It was neat.
I asked, "Who has to approve the card design?" He blinked. Security has to sign off, and they meet on Thursdays. I asked about testing the card printer; it hadn't been used since last year. And the blank cards come from a supplier in another city: four working days, minimum.
He went quiet and started writing in the margin. By the end, Wednesday had become the Wednesday after next.
I'm Jaya, by the way, and I did the same thing in my first year with a canteen contract. Nobody plans the waiting. It's always the waiting.

qa.q: On which day does the security team meet?
qa.a: They meet on Thursdays.

qa.q: How does Jaya seem to feel watching Akash's plan change?
qa.a: Jaya seems sympathetic rather than critical, remembering making the same mistake with a canteen contract.

qa.q: What should Akash add to future plans?
qa.a: Approvals, testing and waiting times, such as security sign-off, printer checks and supplier delivery, since those steps eat the schedule.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt as Wednesday became the Wednesday after next?
qa.a: Akash probably felt deflated and a little embarrassed, having been pleased with a neat plan that missed the hidden steps.

grounding: An observer senior sees a junior's plan leave out approvals, testing and waiting time, the connecting steps that usually eat the schedule.

passage:
Parveen, you asked how I moved my parents from Kanpur to Pune without a single disaster. I'm Reena, and I did it backwards.
The one fixed date was 1 June: the new flat's handover. So I asked, what has to be true on 31 May? The truck loaded, the old flat empty. For that, the movers had to be booked by the 15th, because in summer they're full. For the truck to take the furniture, Papa's cupboards had to be emptied by the 25th, and Papa takes a week to sort one drawer, so we started on the 10th.
Then the gas connection: cancelling takes ten days, so I applied on the 12th. The bank address change needs the new rent agreement, so the landlord had to send it by the 5th.
When I reached today, the plan said: start on 3 May. It was already 4 May. I phoned the landlord that afternoon.
Working backwards showed me the real start date, and all the people I was waiting on.

qa.q: What was the one fixed date?
qa.a: 1 June: the new flat's handover.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when the plan said to start on 3 May?
qa.a: Reena probably felt a jolt of alarm, realising the real start date had already passed, and acted quickly.

qa.q: Why did working backwards help Reena more than starting from today?
qa.a: It showed the true start date and every dependency on other people, like the movers, the landlord and the gas office.

qa.q: How might Reena's father have felt about starting on his cupboards so early?
qa.a: Papa might have grumbled at first but been relieved not to rush, since he takes a week to sort one drawer.

grounding: Illustrates a planner who starts from the deadline and asks what must be true one step earlier, exposing the real start date and dependencies.

passage:
On the day of the Diwali mela in Kudal village, Parveen sat on the courtyard floor with a lump of clay. "One diya for Ammi. Five minutes," she told Tenzin, already in his new shirt.
"The bus goes at four."
"Five minutes."
The clay cracked. She wet it and started again. The spout fell over. She scratched a pattern with a twig, rubbed it off because it was crooked, and did it again.
Tenzin waited on the step, walked to the gate and back, and waited again.
When Parveen held up a small, lopsided diya, the shadows had crossed the courtyard. A bell in the next village rang five.
"Five minutes?" Tenzin said.
Parveen's mouth fell open. "But… it was only five minutes!"

qa.q: At what time did the bus go?
qa.a: The bus goes at four.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when she heard the bell ring five?
qa.a: Parveen felt shocked and surprised, sure it had only been five minutes.

qa.q: What could help Parveen next time she says "five minutes"?
qa.a: Parveen could ask a grown-up to set a timer or check the clock, since it is hard to feel how long making something really takes.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel while waiting?
qa.a: Tenzin was impatient and restless, walking to the gate and back while the time for the bus passed.

grounding: Illustrates a child who sincerely promises a clay diya will take five minutes and is surprised when more than an hour has gone.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Monday. The inter-school short film contest wanted a three-minute film by Saturday. Rashmi pictured it all: film on Thursday after school, edit on Friday night, submit Saturday morning. "Two evenings, easy," she told her friend Bhupen. She didn't think of the last time, when a two-minute class video had taken a week.
Thursday. Rain. The park where she wanted to film was flooded. Bhupen had tuition till six. When they finally shot indoors at seven, the phone memory filled up after four scenes. They deleted old photos and shot again. The light was bad.
Saturday. Rashmi edited from midnight to 4 a.m. The music didn't match the scenes. The export failed twice. She submitted at 11:52, eight minutes before the deadline, with a jump in the sound she had no time to fix.
On the form, it asked, "How long did this take?" She laughed tiredly and wrote, "Longer than I imagined."

qa.q: By when did the contest want the film?
qa.a: By Saturday.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel as she typed on the form?
qa.a: Rashmi felt exhausted and a little rueful, laughing tiredly at how wrong the two-evening estimate had been.

qa.q: What could Rashmi have done when she first estimated the time?
qa.a: Rashmi could have remembered the class video that took a week and started filming earlier, with extra time for weather and technical problems.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Rashmi's "Two evenings, easy"?
qa.a: Bhupen may have believed it at first, but by Thursday night Bhupen would have seen how much the plan ignored real problems.

grounding: Shows a teenager who estimates a film project from the smooth ideal story, starts late and ignores how similar tasks really went.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
I'm Seema, Kunal's mother, and this is the third science project I've watched him start at nine the night before.
At 9:10 he spread chart paper on the floor. By ten he realised he had no glue stick. At 10:40 he asked me to drive him to the stationery shop. It was closed; I knew it would be.
The last two times, I had driven round town, found glue, and stayed up till one cutting pictures. This time I didn't. I made him tea and said, "Use what you have." He used rice paste. The chart was wobbly. He got a C and was annoyed with me for a day.
On Sunday I sat down with him. I didn't lecture. I asked, "When did you find out about this project?" He counted. Twelve days.
We put a small whiteboard by his desk. Every Sunday evening, fifteen minutes: what's due, and what's the first step this week. He rolled his eyes. He also, last week, bought glue on a Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Kunal use instead of a glue stick?
qa.a: He used rice paste.

qa.q: How did Seema seem to feel when she chose not to rescue Kunal this time?
qa.a: Seema seemed torn but determined, choosing tea and "Use what you have" instead of another late-night rescue.

qa.q: What routine did Seema help Kunal build, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes every Sunday evening at a whiteboard to note what is due and the first step, so projects start days earlier.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after getting a C?
qa.a: Kunal felt annoyed, staying cross with his mother for a day.

grounding: A parent watches her teenager cram a project the night before, lets a small consequence teach, and helps him build a weekly starting routine.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
In the architecture studio at the college, it was Wednesday, and the model for the housing project was due on Friday morning. Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.
Keerthana, at the next desk, looked over. "Zainab. You said Monday you'd be done by today."
"I know. But this model is simpler. It's basically boxes."
"Your last model was 'basically a roof.' It took three nights."
Zainab laughed. She had even written an essay on the planning fallacy for her psychology elective last term. She knew every model she had ever made had taken twice as long as she planned. But this time felt different. This time she really could see it in her head.
At 11 p.m. on Thursday, the glue gun jammed. At 2 a.m., one wall wouldn't stand straight. At 6 a.m., she was painting windows with a toothpick.
She submitted at 8:55, eyes red.
"Different this time?" Keerthana asked gently.
"It felt different," Zainab said.

qa.q: How many pieces of mountboard had Zainab cut by Wednesday?
qa.a: Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.

qa.q: Why did Zainab believe this model would be different?
qa.a: Zainab felt hopeful and sure, because this time she could picture it clearly and it seemed simpler.

qa.q: What could Zainab do next time, given her own history?
qa.a: Zainab could plan from how long her past models actually took, about twice her guess, instead of trusting the clear picture in her head.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Zainab's estimate?
qa.a: Keerthana sees the pattern clearly and responds with gentle humour, remembering the "basically a roof" model.

grounding: Shows a student who knows about the planning fallacy and still expects this project to be the exception, and runs late again.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Operations manager's note, Friday.
I watched Nikita, our team lead, have a hard week, and I want to record why.
On Monday, Jaya told Nikita the vendor database would be cleaned by Wednesday. Jaya said this cheerfully and sincerely, the way she has said it before. Nikita built the week around it: training for new staff on Thursday, client reports on Friday.
On Wednesday evening, Jaya said, "Almost done, maybe tomorrow noon." On Thursday it was "end of day." Nikita cancelled the training, apologised to six new staff, and moved the client reports to Monday. I saw her rub her eyes at her desk at seven.
This is the third time this quarter. Nikita told me quietly, "I'd rather Jaya said Friday and meant it."
I have asked Jaya to give estimates using how long the last similar tasks actually took, and to warn Nikita the moment a date is at risk.
— Operations manager

qa.q: When did Jaya say the vendor database would be cleaned?
qa.a: By Wednesday.

qa.q: How was Nikita feeling by Thursday evening?
qa.a: Nikita was tired and frustrated, rubbing her eyes at her desk after cancelling the training and moving the reports.

qa.q: What has the manager asked Jaya to change, and why?
qa.a: To base estimates on how long similar tasks actually took and to warn early, because repeated optimistic dates keep forcing Nikita to reshuffle.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her own dates?
qa.a: Jaya seems to give each date sincerely and cheerfully, probably believing every time that the task will go smoothly.

grounding: Shows a team lead who relies on a colleague's cheerful dates and has to reshuffle repeatedly, as optimism erodes trust.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
subtype: Using past durations and a buffer [Response]
passage:
In the school office, the principal, Mr Nitin Rao, asked Himani, the exam coordinator, when the term-end question papers would be ready. "Can we say the 10th? Parents want the timetable."
Himani's gut said the 10th was fine. Instead, she opened the folder from the last three years. Paper setting had taken nine, eleven and twelve days. Printing had been delayed once by the press and once by a power cut. Two teachers had been on leave each time.
"The last three years, it took eleven days on average, sir. Plus we had one delay every year. I'd say the 15th, with the 13th as our own internal target."
Mr Rao frowned. "The 15th sounds late."
"It sounds late. But the 10th would be based on this year being perfect. It never has been."
He agreed to the 15th. The press was delayed by a day. The papers were ready on the 13th. Mr Rao stopped by her desk with a cup of tea.

qa.q: How long did paper setting take in the last three years?
qa.a: Paper setting had taken nine, eleven and twelve days.

qa.q: How did Mr Rao feel about the 15th at first?
qa.a: Mr Rao was doubtful and a little unhappy, since the 15th sounded late with parents waiting.

qa.q: Why was Himani's estimate more trustworthy than her gut feeling?
qa.a: It was based on how long the task really took in the last three years plus a buffer for the delay that happened every year.

qa.q: How does Mr Rao feel when the papers are ready on the 13th?
qa.a: Mr Rao feels pleased and grateful, stopping by Himani's desk with a cup of tea.

grounding: Illustrates a planner who estimates from how long past tasks actually took and adds a buffer, instead of trusting a confident feeling.

passage:
Dear Diary,
On Sunday I started a plant diary. Jyoti didi gave me a packet of bean seeds and a cup. I drew the cup with a ruler. I wrote "Day 1" in green pen with stars. I was SO excited.
Day 2, I drew the cup again. Nothing had happened. Day 3, same. Day 4 I forgot.
Today is Day 9. There is a tiny green hook coming out of the soil! But my diary has only three pages, and Days 4 to 8 are empty.
Jyoti didi said, "The boring days are part of the story too." I don't think boring days are a story. But I drew the green hook very carefully.
Maybe tomorrow I'll just write one line.
Harsha

qa.q: What did Jyoti didi give Harsha?
qa.a: A packet of bean seeds and a cup.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel on Day 1 compared with Days 2 and 3?
qa.a: Harsha felt very excited on Day 1, but on Days 2 and 3 the diary felt boring because nothing had happened.

qa.q: What small plan might help Harsha keep going through the flat middle?
qa.a: Writing just one line each day, even when nothing changes, as Harsha decides for tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Jyoti didi feel seeing the empty pages?
qa.a: Jyoti didi might feel a bit amused and understanding, and gently encourage Harsha to keep going.

grounding: Illustrates a child who starts a plant diary with great excitement and drops it when nothing seems to happen in the middle.

passage:
In their flat in Mylapore, Ganga's shelf told the story. A half-knitted blue scarf on its needles since August. A coding course on her laptop, stuck at 40%. A skipping rope, and a fitness chart on the wall that stopped on day eleven.
On Saturday, she came in excited. "I'm going to learn calligraphy! Look, I found a pen set online."
Her brother Kishore, home from college, looked at the shelf, then at her. "What about the scarf?"
"It got boring. The middle part is just rows and rows."
"And the course?"
"Loops. So boring. Calligraphy is different."
He didn't laugh. "Ganga, you always say that. Everything is exciting on day one."
She opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the scarf. "Maybe I'm just someone who doesn't finish things."
"Or you've never finished one yet. Pick one. Just one."
She sighed, took down the scarf, and counted the rows left. Forty. "Four rows a day," she said. "Then calligraphy."

qa.q: How far had Ganga got in the coding course?
qa.a: Stuck at 40%.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when she looked at the scarf after Kishore's comment?
qa.a: Ganga felt doubtful and a little ashamed, wondering if she was someone who doesn't finish things.

qa.q: What plan does Ganga make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Four rows of the scarf a day before starting calligraphy, which makes the dull middle small and finishable.

qa.q: How does Kishore see Ganga's new calligraphy idea?
qa.a: Kishore sees it as the same pattern of exciting starts, but he responds kindly and nudges her to finish just one thing.

grounding: Shows a teenager with several half-finished projects who keeps chasing new excitement, until she chooses to push one through its dull stretch.
